Very interesting look at the intersection of faith and morality, and how human nature plays with what is right and wrong in a religious sense. Nobody is perfect, and our mistakes are what makes us human The cinematography here is so good. The scenery inside the cathedrals and churches are so beautiful, and everything is framed so beautifully. Fantastic long shots, great framing showing loneliness and emptiness even in this fantastically rich and over the top setting The score is really nice. For some reason it just goes so well with the vibe of a conclave, and adds really nice tension in almost an elegant way I would have liked more development inside of the actual conclave discussions. The votes were given such a big part, and I don't think there was enough drama and explanation as to who was voting for who and why. We didnt see any courtship, or deliberation, or anything. A vote happened, a skeleton came out for a front runner, and the votes all changed. To me it could have been explored further There were some really beautiful scenes with powerful monolaugues. I specifically think of the scene in the theater, the scene with them all walking with the umbrellas, and the opening scene with the dead pope The messaging was good in the literal aspect, but I felt the way it was done was pretty performative. There was no real buildup for the big twist at the end, and while I love the idea it just felt so poorly done to me I also feel like there was not enough explored religiously. Some surface level themes were there, but I feel there was an opportunity to make some real statements and they shyed away, especially with questioning faith, what makes us faithful, who deserves to be treated how, etc.

This movie is at least 10% of the reason I want to be Catholic. I really enjoyed the setting, it has a really good vibe that I just liked a lot. The plot is fantastic, with a lot of tension points which were great,and a lot of very good twists. I really liked the messages this film had to offer, and I felt like they really spoke to me in a deep way. The characters were well written and felt decently realistic, and I liked the way the movie framed sensitive issues in a way that felt both progressive, but still true to Catholicism and Christianity as a whole. The overarching mystery received a lot of pushback, which I was expecting when I saw it, but I feel like it was undeserved. I don’t have much more to say about the movie, mainly because of how I don’t remember any parts I didn’t like, so it’s hard to elaborate on anything else. I would absolutely watch this movie again, as I feel like there are certain parts that would be elevated on a rewatch. 3.5 out of 4 stars for general enjoyment 1 out of 1 star for rewatch ability 4.5 stars total

Oh, I’m honestly in shock. This film is absolutely fascinating, and I’d recommend it regardless of what you believe. The acting is simply phenomenal, and the score works in such perfect synergy with the visuals. It knows exactly when to emphasize a moment, create tension, or leave you with a sense of mystery. The story itself feels like a small detective mystery intertwined with political intrigue, tangled destinies, and genuine character development. I was particularly impressed by how the characters evolve throughout the film, how their perspectives and perceptions change, and how we’re gradually presented with new details that reshape our understanding of the people we thought we knew. I also loved getting a glimpse into the inner workings of a Vatican conclave: how a pope is elected, the traditions, and all the behind-the-scenes politics. It’s fascinating in its own right. Throughout the film, I found myself repeatedly admiring what I was watching. At one point, I genuinely thought, This is a 9/10. And then... the final twist happened. I won’t spoil it, but my jaw was on the floor. I was completely blindsided. I genuinely have no words. I don’t even know how to feel about this film anymore. It doesn’t erase everything the movie accomplished before that, but the ending clashes deeply with my personal beliefs. My personal take: if you cut the last 15 minutes, this would have been perfect.

Conclave feels like a story about the difference between faith and certainty. It takes place inside one of the most powerful religious institutions in the world, but the film is less interested in religion itself than in what happens when human beings convince themselves they understand something greater than them. What makes the film resonate is how every cardinal carries his own idea of truth. They speak about God, tradition, and morality, but underneath those beliefs are ambition, fear, ego, and insecurity. The conclave becomes a reminder that even the most sacred institutions are still operated by imperfect people. Lawrence is what gives the story its emotional weight. His crisis of faith isn't portrayed as weakness. If anything, his doubt makes him one of the few people capable of genuine reflection. The film quietly suggests that certainty can be more dangerous than disbelief because certainty leaves no room for humility. What lingers is the idea that faith might require doubt. To believe while acknowledging you could be wrong is completely different from using belief as proof of your own righteousness. The characters most convinced of their moral purity often seem the least capable of questioning themselves. The final revelation reinforces everything the film has been asking. Humanity constantly tries to create categories, rules, and structures to make existence easier to understand. But life has never been obligated to fit neatly inside them. Conclave stays with me because it suggests that maybe the opposite of faith isn't doubt. Maybe it's certainty. The moment you believe you have all the answers is often the moment you stop searching for truth.

On rewatch, Conclave is still good but I am noticing a lot of the cracks in the film. My main issues are that the score is so out of touch with the tone of the film that it took me out several times and the plot did have a few too many conveniences that made the lead up to the conclusion rather disatisfying even if that conclusion itself was quite good. The technical aspects of this film are solid but not too standout, with the cinematography having its moments but mostly it was a showcase of the phenomenal production design. The best parts of the film are still the dialogue and the performances, with everything feeling so strangly natural in the best way while continuing to be fun and engaging. Still a great movie even if my opinion on it has lowered since my first viewing of it.

Holy smokes: you just can't beat cardinals ripping clouds and chatting shit in the smoking area. Conclave is beautiful in every way; a mystery of many locked boxes and a ritual of politics & grief that flows between ecclesiastical drama, internal struggle and the quiet mundane. The framing and design of the architecture show a hostile opulence across time, that which secludes and outlives all, just as each marble hotel room bears witness to just a few nights of its occupant's life. An ancient ritual persists with electronic locks and x-ray security, espresso machines and hotel toiletries. Just as much attention is given to the bus ride and meals times as rounds of voting - each process is just as important in how it determines who will be the spiritual leader of m/billions. Through the mundanities, the conclave is demystified; however, we are still kept at arms reach, barred not only from participation, but knowledge of every other iteration, left to wonder about the thousands of cardinals (and sisters) of the Curia throughout history, the decisions made and the influence they have had on world events. The very brief extract of choral music we get is just divine, it's no wonder pre-modern folks heard the beauty of the heavens in it as it echoed through those high ceilings. The homily that follows is such a beautiful (hopeful) distillation of faith in the modern age, faith as something that breathes and changes, something human that should be in conversation with doubt and interpretation, a united church of mutual respect and integration and openness. In order to believe, one must accept that they cannot fully understand. Interspersed with grand affairs of scandal, there's a real tenderness to the scenes in between: the stillness of a dead man's room, left lived-in and undisturbed; letting yourself feel the grief of a dear friend lost when you has to keep it together for so long; asking someone to quietly pray with you while you're whole world is falling down. Bit of a tacked-on twist ending, but that's the book's fault, and apparently the author has been locked into a twisty Shyamalan brand that harms his ability to tell a good story. Nevertheless, through this and his other interactions with Cardinal Benitez, Cardinal Lawrence, a Church 'Liberal', is able to truly heed his own words. I know it would be hard to track, but I really feel like you shouldn't be able to vote for yourself in the conclave...
